entries.gloss: Striving against the lower or disordering tendencies of the self so the person is formed toward obedience, virtue, and nearness to God.
The self or inner dimension of the human person discussed in relation to desire, discipline, repentance, and spiritual formation.
The commanding self: the tendency of desire to press a person toward what is forbidden or spiritually harmful when it is not governed.
Patience, endurance, and steadiness under difficulty, temptation, or duty; the book treats it as something that can become a stable disposition.
Repentance: recognizing wrongdoing, regretting it, turning away from it, and repairing what can be repaired.
Inner expansiveness or breadth of chest: remaining open, composed, and constructive rather than narrowed by anger, insult, or pressure.
A means by which wrongdoing or its consequences are addressed through prescribed or morally corrective acts.
Worship and servitude to God, presented as a way of orienting the whole person toward God rather than as isolated rituals.
Sincerity: orienting an act toward God rather than making reputation, praise, status, or approval its real purpose.
Remembrance of God through verbal and inward attention; presented as a practical force for sustaining God-consciousness.
Reliance upon God while still fulfilling responsibilities and taking appropriate means; trust in the outcome, not abandonment of effort.
Divine oneness; the final unit distinguishes dimensions including essence, attributes, worship, and action.
God-consciousness expressed as vigilance in choices and restraint from what distances a person from God.
Treating failure or sin as grounds for giving up hope, making further reform less likely.
Putting repentance or necessary reform off until later, allowing delay itself to become a barrier to change.
Natural drives and inclinations. The book argues for their regulation and proper direction rather than indiscriminate destruction.
Long-term shaping of the person through knowledge, repeated practice, restraint, repentance, worship, and divine orientation.
Governance of impulses and desires so a person can choose what is right instead of simply obeying the strongest immediate inclination.
Repentance is incomplete when wrongdoing has created obligations toward other people that remain unaddressed.
Treating speech as an arena of self-control: truth, timing, intention, audience, and consequences all matter.
Education is more than information transfer: teaching should contribute to moral and spiritual formation.
Tawakkul does not erase human responsibility; the person acts and uses means while entrusting ultimate effectiveness and outcome to God.
